clips.title: 7 Cryptography Concepts EVERY Developer Should Know
clips.why: Fireship explains hashing with Node's own crypto module, which is exactly the tool the broker uses for capabilities.
look: createHash in Node: the same input always gives the same digest.
Why a hash cannot be turned back into its input, which is why storing digests is safe.
How a hash is used to check a value without storing the value itself.
clips.after: The broker stores only sha256(capability) and checks every request by hashing the token it was shown.

clips.title: I Cracked a Password using ONLY Response Times...
clips.why: A real timing attack, step by step: a normal string comparison leaks how much of a guess was right.
look: Why a comparison that stops at the first wrong character takes longer for better guesses.
How the attack first finds the length of the key, then one character at a time.
How the guessed key grows one character at a time, because the slowest answer gives each character away.
clips.after: This is why the broker never compares a capability with ===.

clips.title: I Cracked a Password using ONLY Response Times...
clips.why: The fix in under a minute: compare in constant time, the idea behind the Node function this lesson uses.
look: The constant-time comparison. In Node it is timingSafeEqual from node:crypto.
clips.after: matches() hashes first and then calls timingSafeEqual, so both sides are always 32 bytes and the time says nothing.

clips.title: 7 Cryptography Concepts EVERY Developer Should Know
clips.why: For the Go deeper panel: HMAC, a hash mixed with a secret key, which is how the gateway's run tokens are signed.
look: createHmac with a key: only someone with the key can produce the same signature.
clips.after: The gateway checks a run token by computing the HMAC of its claims again and comparing the two with timingSafeEqual.

practice.q: Which line makes a capability that nobody can guess?

options.why: Math.random is built for speed, its outputs can be predicted, and this gives only a few characters.
32 secure random bytes from the operating system, written as 64 hex characters: far too many possibilities to guess.
A hash of a known value is as guessable as the value. Anyone who knows the run id can compute it.

practice.q: Finish matches() so it compares in constant time and never throws on a short guess.
practice.before:
export const matches = (presented: string, digest: Buffer) =>
  timingSafeEqual(
practice.hint: Turn the presented text into 32 bytes first.
practice.why: Hashing first gives two 32-byte digests, so timingSafeEqual never sees different lengths and the time says nothing.

practice.q: The broker's table of digests leaks. What can an attacker do with it?

options.text: Call the broker as any open run
options.why: The broker hashes what it is shown. The hash of a digest is a different digest, so it matches nothing.

options.text: Turn the digests back into capabilities
options.why: A hash only works in one direction, and a 256-bit random input cannot be found by guessing.

options.text: Nothing useful: the digests are not passes and cannot be reversed
options.why: That is why the broker stores only digests. The capability itself exists only on the run's machine.

practice.q: Calling timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from("abc"), Buffer.from("abcd")) throws an error. Which one?
practice.after: : Input buffers must have the same byte length
practice.hint: The kind of error JavaScript uses when a value is outside what is allowed.
practice.why: timingSafeEqual needs equal lengths. Comparing digests guarantees that.

practice.q: Put the life of a capability in order.
items: The broker makes it with randomBytes(32)
It stores only sha256(capability) next to the run's scope
It hands the capability to the run's machine once
A request arrives with Authorization: Bearer <capability>
The broker hashes the token and compares digests with timingSafeEqual
The run ends and the scope is revoked
practice.why: The capability itself is never stored or logged by the broker. Only its digest stays, and only until the run ends.
